solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Element of choice covering a container

indicators.note: the outer word wraps over the rest, covering it from both sides

parts.note: the plum is the choicest pick, so plum means choice
a tin is a container

explanation.surface: A chemistry note about picking an element to coat some vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Platinum is a chemical element, a precious metal with the symbol Pt.

clue.text: What flows from below via arterioles

indicators.note: in a down clue, reading from below means reading upwards, backwards
via says the answer travels by way of the letters inside the next word

parts.note: the run sits inside this word

explanation.surface: An anatomy line about blood moving up through small arteries.
explanation.walkthrough: The bloodstream picture makes 'What flows' sound like blood; it is a river. ERIOL sits inside 'arterioles', and read upwards it gives the French river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Loire is France's longest river, and a river is a thing that flows.

clue.text: Lands finally at the other far island with some MPs

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of each of the four words that follow

parts.note: I is the map abbreviation for island
Tories are Conservative members of the UK Parliament, so some of its MPs

explanation.surface: Travel notes about landing at a distant island alongside a group of politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes the last letter of each of 'at the other far', giving TERR. The Tories are Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Territories are lands or regions under a particular government's control.

clue.text: King leaving piece on grate for bird

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part sits on top of the second
the king's letter departs from the word, so it is taken out

parts.note: a knight is a chess piece
K is the chess abbreviation for king
to grate on someone is to jar

explanation.surface: A king walks away from a log set on the fire grate.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'grate' looks like a fireplace grate; it is the verb, as in a noise that grates on the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The nightjar is a nocturnal bird known for its churring call.

clue.text: Fiendish Bard character loading shipment at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Ophelia is a character in Hamlet, by Shakespeare, the Bard

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare character packing cargo on board a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loading' joins OPHELIA to SHIPMENT; the combined letters are then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Mephistopheles is the devil of the Faust legend, so the adjective means devilish or wickedly cunning.

clue.text: Language centre for Hebrew school

indicators.note: centre for picks the two middle letters of the six-letter word

parts.note: Eton is a famous English public school

explanation.surface: A language centre attached to a Hebrew school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Language centre' reads as one institution, but the language is the definition and 'centre' does the work. Eton is a famous English school.
explanation.definitionFit: Breton is the Celtic tongue spoken in Brittany, in north-west France.

clue.text: Aristocrat upset over profit cap

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part is placed over the second
in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the word reads upwards

parts.note: a nob is an upper-class person, an aristocrat
net profit, the amount after costs, so net means profit

explanation.surface: An aristocrat cross about a cap on profits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cap' looks like a limit on profit; it is headwear.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonnet is a type of hat, so a kind of cap or head covering.

clue.text: Uses fingers to investigate skinned fish

indicators.note: skinned means its outer letters are stripped off both ends

parts.note: someone who explores by touch feels

explanation.surface: Someone probing a skinned fish with their fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: An eel is a long snake-like fish.

clue.text: Suitable work on harbour, one in Marseille

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part sits on top of what follows

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work
a port is a harbour
une is French for one, and Marseille is in France

explanation.surface: Fitting work on a harbour, perhaps in the French port of Marseille.
explanation.definitionFit: Opportune means well-timed or appropriate to the occasion.

clue.text: Platform 10 recalled by backward youth

indicators.note: by means beside, so one part sits next to the other
recalled means called back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: the figures 1 and 0 look like the letters I and O

indicators.note: backward means the letters run the other way

parts.note: a girl is a youth

explanation.surface: A platform number announced again by a shy young person.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' looks like a cross-reference to 10-across; it is the letters I and O. Read back it gives OI, and GIRL read back gives LRIG.
explanation.definitionFit: An oil rig is a drilling platform, often out at sea.

clue.text: Hero's wife and writer do a bunk

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument, a writer
do a bunk is British slang for run away, as eloping lovers do

explanation.surface: A hero's wife and an author run off together.
explanation.walkthrough: To do a bunk is British slang for running away secretly.
explanation.definitionFit: Penelope is the faithful wife of Odysseus, hero of Homer's Odyssey.

clue.text: Whale bites male in half

definitions.note: semi is a prefix meaning half

indicators.note: the whale's letters close round the other letter as if biting it

parts.note: the sei is a species of whale

explanation.surface: A whale bites a man in two.
explanation.walkthrough: The sei is a baleen whale, a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: Semi- is the prefix for half, as in semicircle; semi is also short for a semifinal.

clue.text: Crops enclosing compound for quarterly periods

indicators.note: the first word goes round the second, enclosing it

parts.note: to crop is to trim, so crops means trims
an ester is a chemical compound

explanation.surface: A farming note about crops kept in a compound, counted by the quarter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crops' reads as a noun for harvests; it is the verb, as in cropping hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A trimester is a three-month span, a quarter of a year, so these are quarterly periods.

clue.text: Food Day in Berlin? Follow up on magazine

indicators.note: in a down clue these letters sit on top of the next part

parts.note: Tag is German for day

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word reads upwards, backwards

parts.note: to tail someone is to follow them
Elle is a fashion magazine

explanation.surface: A German day of following up a story in a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: TAIL read upwards gives LIAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Tagliatelle is a ribbon pasta, a food from Italy.

clue.text: 'Liqueur' changed to 'Cava' on promotion

indicators.note: in an across clue the rearranged letters follow, as if placed on what comes first

parts.note: an ad is a promotion, an advertisement

indicators.note: changed tells us the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wine list where a liqueur is swapped for cava in a sales push.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like an editing note; only 'Liqueur' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Advocaat is a Dutch liqueur made with eggs, sugar and brandy.

clue.text: Dean's band perhaps in gold playing with Carol

definitions.note: a cleric's white collar band, worn by a dean among others

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters fooling about into a new order

explanation.surface: A dean's band playing gold discs with someone called Carol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' suggests musicians, but it is a strip of cloth round the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog collar is the stiff white collar worn by clergy, such as a dean of a cathedral.

clue.text: Excess cheek parents essentially ignored

indicators.note: ignored means the letter is left out

parts.note: a glute is a buttock muscle, and cheek is slang for a buttock

indicators.note: essentially points to the very heart of the word, its central letter

explanation.surface: Too much cheek from children, with parents taking no notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cheek' looks like impudence; it is a buttock, the glute. The central letter of 'parents' is E, removed from GLUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A glut is an oversupply, more of something than is needed.

clue.text: Old fellow south of pole to see ancient beast

indicators.note: in a down clue south of means placed below

parts.note: a mast is a pole
a don is a university fellow

explanation.surface: An old man at the South Pole going to see a prehistoric animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'south of pole' suggests Antarctica; it just places O and DON below MAST.
explanation.definitionFit: The mastodon is an extinct elephant-like mammal.

clue.text: Fruit from the East one regularly flags up

indicators.note: read from the east, in an across clue, means right to left, backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: regularly picks every other letter, the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.surface: A fruit from the Orient, flagged up at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: Every other letter of 'flags up' gives LGU; after I that is ILGU, read from the right.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit, a cross of grapefruit and tangerine.

clue.text: Idiot endlessly ranks confectionery

indicators.note: without its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: prat is British slang for an idiot
ranks are lines of soldiers

explanation.surface: A fool keeps grading sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: Prat is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Pralines are sweets of nuts cooked in sugar, a type of confectionery.

clue.text: Part of prince's cortege paid for accompaniment

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone in a royal procession being paid to come along.
explanation.definitionFit: An escort can be a companion hired for a social occasion.

clue.text: Happy to hold relative steady

indicators.note: the outer word wraps round the other, holding it

parts.note: content means happy, satisfied
sis, short for sister, is a relative

explanation.surface: Someone glad to keep a family member on an even keel.
explanation.definitionFit: Consistent means unchanging and reliable, never erratic.

clue.text: Doctor following to resting place

indicators.note: following means these letters come after the other word

parts.note: MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: A doctor following someone to their final rest.
explanation.walkthrough: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a British doctor's qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomb is a grave or vault, a final resting place for the dead.

clue.text: One with tablets treating some symptoms at last

indicators.note: treating suggests processing, working the letters over into a new order
at last picks the final letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A patient with pills, treating a few symptoms in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tablets' suggests pills; they are the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments. SOME is rearranged and the last letter of 'symptoms' follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Moses brought the Ten Commandments down from Sinai on two stone tablets.

clue.text: Pleased with exposure of Fiddle and Flowers

parts.note: glad means pleased

indicators.note: exposure strips off the outer layer, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: a fiddle is a violin

explanation.surface: Delighted to show off a violin and a bunch of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: VIOLIN without its outer letters gives IOLI.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladioli are tall garden plants with spikes of flowers.

clue.text: Thick mass beneath surfaces of drains inspected

indicators.note: in a down clue beneath means placed below the other part
the surface of each word is its top, its first letter in a down clue

parts.note: M is the physics symbol for mass

explanation.surface: Thick sludge found under the surfaces of drains that were checked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thick' sounds like sludge; it means stupid.
explanation.definitionFit: Dim is informal for slow-witted, as thick is.

clue.text: Tasty 6 extracted from 5

indicators.note: extracted from means pulled out of the word that follows

parts.note: 5-down's definition is Fiendish, and fiendish means devilish
VI is the Roman numeral for six

explanation.surface: A cookery note that something tasty can be taken out of a fiendish dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers look like cross-references to 6 and 5; '6' is just the Roman numeral, and '5' stands for its definition, fiendish, so devilish. Taking six out leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Delish is informal shorthand for delicious.

clue.text: Help given with a line dance by trainer

parts.note: a prom is a formal dance
PT is physical training, so a PT is a fitness trainer

explanation.surface: A trainer at a dance helps someone who has forgotten their lines.
explanation.walkthrough: PT, physical training, is how British schools named PE; a PT is also a personal trainer.
explanation.definitionFit: In theatre a prompt is the cue fed to an actor who forgets a line.

clue.text: Foolish son seen eating new rhubarb

definitions.note: rhubarb is British slang for nonsense

indicators.note: eating means the rearranged letters take the other letter into their middle, as if swallowing it
foolish suggests the letters are behaving daftly and mixed up

explanation.surface: A silly son spotted eating fresh rhubarb.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'son seen' are rearranged with N tucked inside them. Rhubarb is British slang for nonsense, from actors muttering the word as crowd noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhubarb is informal for meaningless talk, drivel.
